title: Ask what would make anyone act so
statement: Ask what would make anyone act as a character did, not what would make the learner, and check the answer against a clue the text prints.
detail: Lesson research on motive questions, reading a literature review of inference teaching, found that a reader's own background changes the inferences they draw, and that even on texts designed to produce one agreed inference some readers inferred emotions that were the precise opposite of the one intended. The character-motivation variation of the course's inference procedure asks what would make me do what the character did, which the research says invites exactly this projection. It recommends the general form, what would make anyone do that, with the answer then checked back against a printed clue, and the lesson plan adopts the general form. The same research has scoring accept any motive tied to a real clue, with the accept-list written from the clues.
against: The research note was "Written before the lesson is authored." (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/research/g4-u1-l3-circe-and-the-lotus-eaters.md`, line 9), and no result with learners is recorded for either wording.

evidence.quote: Narvaez's work reported in the review found that a reader's own moral and cultural background changes the inferences they draw while reading

even on texts designed to produce one agreed inference "there was no consensus. In fact some readers inferred emotions that were the precise opposite of that intended" (Kispal, quoting Gygax et al. 2004).

That wording invites exactly this failure. My recommendation is to keep the variation but voice it in the general form, what would make anyone do that, and then require the answer to be checked back against a printed clue. Second, single-correct motive items are riskier than they look, so the scoring of the child's written motive must accept any reason that is tied to a real clue, and the accept-list has to be written from the clues rather than from one exemplar sentence.
Step 3 is where the variation is amended: its published wording is if that happened to me, what would make me do what the character did, and this lesson voices it in the general form instead.
Written before the lesson is authored.
the character-motivation variation says step 3 is "If that happened to me, what would make me do what the character did?". That wording invites exactly this failure.
My recommendation is to keep the variation but voice it in the general form, what would make anyone do that, and then require the answer to be checked back against a printed clue.
Step 3 is voiced in the general form, never the first person.
Do not write if that happened to me, do not write how would you feel, and do not write anything that asks the child to supply their own reaction.
